1956: Awarded on 18 December 1956, just ahead of Alfredo Di Stéfano; presented at a civic reception at Blackpool Town Hall.
Aged 41 years, 10 months and 17 days – still the oldest winner (men and women).
Season before the award: led Blackpool to their highest league finish in 25 years, runners-up to Manchester United's 'Busby Babes'.
No team title in the calendar year – the first winner to win without one.
Played on until 50, retiring on 6 February 1965 with Stoke City (3–1 v Fulham).
1957: Won with 72 points; Billy Wright 19, Duncan Edwards and Raymond Kopa 16 each – one of the most emphatic wins.
Also won the European Cup that year with Real Madrid.
Spain then failed to qualify for the 1958 World Cup, so the reigning winner missed it.
1959: Second win, making him the first player to win the Ballon d'Or twice.
Also won the European Cup that year with Real Madrid.
1958: Also won the European Cup that year with Real Madrid.
1958 World Cup: 3 goals, France finished third (lost to Brazil in the semi-final); named in the tournament's all-star team.
1960: Won the award while playing for FC Barcelona – the club's first Ballon d'Or; the 5th winner overall.
1961: Collected the award in December 1961 after firing Juventus to back-to-back Serie A titles.
Born in Argentina; won the 1957 South American Championship with Argentina (named best player), then played for Italy from 1961 (8 goals in 9 games).
At the 1962 World Cup, Italy went out in the group stage.
1962: Won in the year of the 1962 World Cup: scored the opening goal in the final against Brazil (lost 3–1), won the Silver Ball and made the Team of the Tournament.
Played for Dukla Prague; Czechoslovakia had five Ballon d'Or-nominated players in that final.
1963: The only goalkeeper ever to win the Ballon d'Or.
1963 Soviet league season: conceded just 6 goals in 27 matches for Dynamo Moscow.
Won with 73 points, ahead of Gianni Rivera and Jimmy Greaves. (Rivera later said he was told he had been leading and the award went to Yashin 'for his overall career'.)
Before this: 1956 Olympic gold and the first European Championship (1960) with the Soviet Union.
1964: Won despite a trophyless season (no team title that year).
Played for Manchester United (per that year's ranking).
1965: First player born in Africa to win the award (born in Mozambique); played for Benfica.
Over 14 years at Benfica: 11 league titles, 5 Portuguese Cups, 7 times league top scorer, over 700 goals.
The following summer (1966 World Cup) he was top scorer with 9 goals and Portugal took third place.
1966: Won the World Cup with England the same year – the first player to win both; scored 3 goals at the tournament, including twice in the semi-final against Portugal.
Won the FWA Footballer of the Year weeks before the World Cup.
Went into the tournament with 37 international goals in 64 appearances.
1968: Also won the European Cup that year with Manchester United (beat Benfica at Wembley).
Aged 22 years and 212 days – the 4th-youngest winner.
1969: Won after AC Milan won the European Cup (4–1 v Ajax) and then the Intercontinental Cup v Estudiantes (3–0, 1–2); he was Milan's captain and No. 10.
Aged 26; learned of the award after Christmas, through the newspapers.
Had won Euro 1968 with Italy the year before.
1970: Won after the 1970 World Cup in Mexico, where he was top scorer with 10 goals; West Germany finished 3rd.
No team title that calendar year (a 'trophyless' winner, per the site).
1967: The only Hungarian ever to win the Ballon d'Or; played for Ferencváros (per that year's ranking).
1971: First of his three wins (1971, 1973, 1974), as an Ajax player.
Also won the European Cup that year with Ajax.
1972: Won with 81 points – Gerd Müller and Günter Netzer both had 79: the closest three-way race in the award's history.
Won Euro 1972 with West Germany that year; Bayern Munich were in their era of dominance.
1973: Moved from Ajax to FC Barcelona in summer 1973 and still won – one of seven winners to win straight after a summer transfer.
Also won the European Cup that year with Ajax (before the move).
1974: Captained the Netherlands to the 1974 World Cup final (lost to West Germany); the standout player of the tournament, introduced the 'Cruyff Turn', led the semi-final win over Brazil.
1976: Second win, as a Bayern Munich player; also won the European Cup that year – Bayern won three in a row.
Had captained West Germany to the 1974 World Cup in between his two wins.
1975: Played for Dynamo Kyiv (per that year's ranking).
1977: Won with 74 points; Kevin Keegan 71, Michel Platini 70 – one of the narrowest margins.
Scored for Borussia Mönchengladbach in the 1977 European Cup final (against Keegan's Liverpool).
Denmark then failed to qualify for the 1978 World Cup.
1987: Won the Eredivisie with PSV Eindhoven, then became AC Milan's record signing that summer – won the award in the year of his transfer.
1995: Champions League top scorer with Paris Saint-Germain, then moved to AC Milan in the summer – won in the year of his transfer.
Won with 144 points; Jürgen Klinsmann 108, Jari Litmanen 67. Announced on 26 December 1995.
The first year the award was open to all nationalities – first (and still only) African winner.
Won the Coupe de France and Coupe de la Ligue with PSG in 1995 (from his honours list).
1997: Scored 47 goals in 49 matches for Barcelona in 1996–97 and won the Copa del Rey, the Spanish Super Cup and the European Cup Winners' Cup.
Moved to Inter Milan in summer 1997 for a then-record fee and kept scoring.
Won the 1997 Copa América with Brazil and was Player of the Tournament.
Youngest winner ever: 21 years and 92 days. Top 3: Ronaldo, Predrag Mijatović, Zinédine Zidane.
2000: Shone for Barcelona and at Euro 2000 with Portugal, then made 'the transfer of the century' to Real Madrid and won the award that year.
Won despite a trophyless season (no team title).
Won with 197 points, 18 ahead of Zinedine Zidane (who won Euro 2000 and knocked Portugal out in the semi-final). Awarded on 19 December 2000.
Earned it mostly with Barcelona in the first half of the year, then moved to Real Madrid for a record fee (release clause of 10 billion pesetas); booed on his return to Camp Nou on 21 October 2000.
Reached the Euro 2000 semi-final with Portugal.
2002: Came back from serious injuries at Inter Milan to win the 2002 World Cup and the Golden Boot with Brazil (8 goals, two in the final against Germany).
Signed for Real Madrid that summer and won his second Ballon d'Or months later.
2006: Captained Italy to the 2006 World Cup – the defence conceded just two goals all tournament.
After Juventus were relegated in the Calciopoli scandal he signed for Real Madrid, then won the award.
Won 49 points ahead of Gianluigi Buffon; Thierry Henry 3rd, then Ronaldinho and Zidane.
Third defender ever to win (after Beckenbauer and Sammer) and the first Italian defender.
2021: Won the Copa del Rey with Barcelona and the Copa América with Argentina (the star of the tournament), then moved to PSG – his 7th Ballon d'Or.
Won the Copa América with Argentina – top scorer and best player – ending a 28-year title drought; also won the Copa del Rey with Barcelona, then moved to PSG. 22.7% of the points.
2023: Led Argentina to the 2022 World Cup and won Ligue 1 with PSG; signed for Inter Miami in summer 2023 – the first winner playing outside Europe. His 8th Ballon d'Or.
First award judged on the season (since 2022): 2022-23 season stats – 54 matches, 38 goals, 25 assists.
Won the 2022 World Cup (scored in the final v France) and was named best player of the tournament with 7 goals; also the 2022 Finalissima and Ligue 1 with PSG.
31.3% of the points; Erling Haaland 2nd, Kylian Mbappé 3rd. Aged 36 years, 3 months and 6 days – the oldest winner of the global era.
1978: Won despite a trophyless season (no team title).
Playing for Hamburg (moved from Liverpool after winning the 1977 European Cup); took nearly a quarter of all votes.
2013: Won despite a trophyless season – the most recent winner to do so.
Won with Real Madrid despite a trophyless year – the most recent winner to do so (no Champions League that year).
1979: Second win in a row, at Hamburg – took about 30% of the votes. Inspired Hamburg to a rare Bundesliga title around this period.
1980: First of two wins in a row as a Bayern Munich player.
Won Euro 1980 with West Germany that year and made the Team of the Tournament.
1981: Second win in a row – the last Bundesliga player to win the Ballon d'Or.
1982: Won the 1982 World Cup with Italy in Spain: top scorer (6 goals) and best player of the tournament – scored in the final (3–1 v West Germany) and a hat-trick v Brazil.
Rivera: Rossi 'won his in fifteen days in 1982'. Had missed Euro 1980 through suspension.
1983: Won with 110 points; Kenny Dalglish 26, Allan Simonsen 25 – one of the most emphatic wins.
Serie A top scorer with Juventus – he was top scorer three seasons running (1983–85), matching his three wins.
1984: Captained France to Euro 1984 on home soil – top scorer with 9 of France's 14 goals in 5 games (two perfect hat-tricks, semi-final goal v Portugal, free-kick in the final v Spain) and best player.
Serie A top scorer again with Juventus.
1985: Third win in a row, awarded on Christmas Eve 1985 – also won the European Cup with Juventus that year.
Serie A top scorer for a third season running.
1986: 1986 World Cup: 4 goals and 6 assists for the Soviet Union, including a hat-trick in the 4–3 round-of-16 defeat to Belgium; won the Bronze Boot.
Played for Dynamo Kyiv under Valeri Lobanovskyi.
1988: Won Euro 1988 with the Netherlands: top scorer and best player of the tournament, scored the famous volley in the 2–0 final v USSR (53 touches, 13 duels won, 6 of 7 dribbles).
Had played only 19 matches (8 goals) in his first season at AC Milan, after ankle ligament surgery in November 1987.
Teammate Ruud Gullit captained the Euro 1988 win.
1989: Also won the European Cup with AC Milan; Milan teammate Franco Baresi was runner-up.
1992: Third win: 98 points, ahead of Hristo Stoichkov on 80.
1990: Captained West Germany to the 1990 World Cup title in Italy (1–0 final win over Argentina) and won the Ballon d'Or months later, playing for Inter Milan.
1991: Won with 141 points (32% of the points); Dejan Savićević, Darko Pančev and Lothar Matthäus tied second on 42.
With Marseille: French champions, reached the European Cup final (lost on penalties to Red Star Belgrade – he scored his penalty) and the Coupe de France final.
With France: a perfect record in the Euro 1992 qualifying group; 6 goals in 4 qualifiers in 1991.
Announced on 12 December 1991. Still the only French winner while playing for a French club.
1993: Scored 5 goals in the semi-finals and final of the UEFA Cup, which Juventus won; also scored key goals as Italy qualified for the 1994 World Cup.
Called it 'my big year, the best of all' and Juventus's best year since he joined.
1994: Won with 210 points; Roberto Baggio 136, Paolo Maldini 109. Named on 20 December 1994.
Fourth La Liga title in a row with Barcelona; lost the Champions League final 4–0 to AC Milan.
1994 World Cup: joint top scorer with 6 goals (Golden Boot), Bronze Ball, Team of the Tournament; led Bulgaria to 4th, beating holders Germany 2–1 in the quarter-final. Also 5 goals in qualifying.
1996: Won by a single point – 144 to Ronaldo's 143 – the only time it has been won by one point.
Won Euro 1996 with Germany as the sweeper ('the last great libero'); the site says he scored an extra-time winner v Bulgaria in the quarter-finals.
Played for Borussia Dortmund – the only German winner never to have played for Bayern; the last German winner. Learned he had won from a friend's phone call.
1998: Won with 244 points; Davor Šuker 68, Ronaldo 66 – one of the most emphatic wins.
Won the 1998 World Cup with France, scoring two headers in the final v Brazil.
Won a second Serie A title in a row with Juventus (best attack, 67 goals); he scored 6 league goals.
Lost the Champions League final to Real Madrid a week after the Serie A season – 'one of my greatest disappointments'.
Scored the only goal in the opening match of the Stade de France v Spain (1–0) at the start of 1998.
1999: Led Barcelona to the 1999 La Liga title (his second in a row) and won the 1999 Copa América with Brazil as the tournament's top scorer.
2001: Helped Liverpool win the FA Cup, League Cup and UEFA Cup in 2001.
Scored a hat-trick in England's 5–1 win in Germany on 1 September 2001.
Aged 22 years and 4 days – 2nd-youngest winner; the first Englishman to win since Kevin Keegan.
2003: Won by more than 60 points ahead of Thierry Henry and Paolo Maldini.
Led Juventus to the Champions League final, knocking out Real Madrid in the semi-final, but a late yellow card v Real suspended him for the final (Juve lost to AC Milan).
Called 2003 his best year – played almost the whole season without injury. First winner for the Czech Republic and the 8th for a Juventus player.
2004: Won the Serie A title with AC Milan and was Serie A top scorer (Capocannoniere) with 24 goals.
Strong 2006 World Cup qualifying campaign with Ukraine.
Had won the Champions League with Milan the year before (2003).
2005: Won with 225 points; Frank Lampard 148, Steven Gerrard 142. Awarded on 28 November 2005.
Won La Liga with Barcelona (back-to-back titles in 2005 and 2006 under Frank Rijkaard); also won the 2005 Confederations Cup with Brazil.
Ten days before the award, scored twice in a 3–0 win at the Bernabéu and got a standing ovation from Real Madrid fans.
2007: Won the Champions League with AC Milan and was the competition's top scorer, with decisive goals against Celtic, Bayern Munich and Manchester United (his second goal v United is rated one of the best in the tournament's history).
Won 'by a landslide' – the last Brazilian winner and the last Serie A player to win (as of 2026).
2008: First of five wins, while playing for Manchester United; also won the Champions League that year.
From 2001 on, he and Rodri are the only winners crowned while playing in the English top flight.
2014: Third win, with Real Madrid – also won the Champions League that year. Finished ahead of World Cup finalist Lionel Messi and World Cup winner Manuel Neuer (3rd, 15.72% of the votes).
At the 2014 World Cup that followed, Portugal went out in the group stage.
2016: Fourth win – also won the Champions League with Real Madrid and led Portugal to Euro 2016, the country's first major title.
2017: Fifth win – also won the Champions League with Real Madrid that year.
2009: Won with an overwhelming majority (32.7% of the points). Aged 22 years and 160 days – 3rd-youngest winner.
Scored a header in the 2–0 Champions League final win over Manchester United in Rome, sealing Barcelona's treble under Pep Guardiola.
2010: Second win in a row (22.6% of the points), ahead of World Cup winners Andrés Iniesta and Xavi.
Scored four goals against Arsenal in the Champions League quarter-final.
2011: Won with 47.8% of the points – almost half – ahead of Cristiano Ronaldo (21.6%) and Xavi (9.2%).
Also won the Champions League with Barcelona (final at Wembley); scored the famous solo goal at the Bernabéu in the semi-final first leg v Real Madrid.
2012: Scored 91 goals in the 2012 calendar year – breaking Gerd Müller's record of 85 (set in 1972) with goal 86 v Real Betis in December.
Barcelona only won the Copa del Rey that season. 41.6% of the points – his fourth win in a row.
2015: Barcelona won the treble under Luis Enrique, with Messi, Luis Suárez and Neymar up front; 44.3% of the points.
Scored the goal where Jérôme Boateng fell over, and chipped Manuel Neuer, in the Champions League semi-final v Bayern.
2019: Won with 686 points to Virgil van Dijk's 679 (24.3%) – one of the closest races.

Scored 51 goals and 22 assists in 50 games for Barcelona that season; his 30-metre free-kick v Liverpool in the Champions League semi-final was his 600th Barça goal (Barcelona were then knocked out at Anfield).
His 6th win, breaking the tie with Cristiano Ronaldo.
2018: Won the Champions League with Real Madrid in 2018 (site's same-year Champions League list).
Lost the 2018 World Cup final with Croatia but still finished ahead of Cristiano Ronaldo and Antoine Griezmann (the first 2018 World Cup winner in the ranking).
In his own words: he won his 'individual awards during 2018' before the Ballon d'Or. The site does not list them.
Aged 33 – one of three winners at that age (with Di Stéfano and Cannavaro).
No winning-season match stats (games, goals, assists) on ballondor.com.
2020: No Ballon d'Or was awarded in 2020. The site shows no ranking for this year.
2022: Won the Champions League with Real Madrid, including the 3-1 round-of-16 comeback against PSG that he mentions.
Points: Benzema 549, Sadio Mané 193, Kevin De Bruyne 175, Robert Lewandowski 170, Mohamed Salah 116, Kylian Mbappé 85.
36.8% of the points. The 45th winner of the award. Aged 34 years, 9 months and 29 days.
No winning-season match stats (games, goals, assists) on ballondor.com.
2024: 2023-24 season: 63 matches, 12 goals, 14 assists, 15 yellow cards, 1 red card (France Football interview box).
Won Euro 2024 with Spain and was Player of the Tournament; won the Premier League 2024 with Manchester City.
Collected the trophy on crutches, injured, in late October 2024 at the Théâtre du Châtelet, Paris.
Manchester City's first Ballon d'Or winner. At 1.90 m, the second-tallest winner ever.
2025: 2024-25 season: 60 matches, 37 goals, 15 assists, 5 yellow cards, 1 red card (France Football interview box). Another article on the site says 35 goals.
Won the Champions League with PSG (5-0 v Inter, 31 May 2025), part of a historic quadruple, plus Ligue 1. Scored 8 Champions League goals and assisted twice in the final.
Key games he names: the round-of-16 2nd leg at Anfield (11 March 2025) and the 1-0 semi-final 1st leg at Arsenal, where he scored.
Won the award on his very first nomination. Lamine Yamal 2nd, Vitinha 3rd (per the site's Portugal article). Height 1.78 m – exactly the winners' average.
